lessons.title: Permaculture ethics and design principles
lessons.html:
What permaculture is

Permaculture is a way of designing farms, gardens and settlements so that they work like natural ecosystems: productive, diverse and largely self-sustaining. The word comes from permanent agriculture. It was developed in Australia by Bill Mollison and David Holmgren and is used by many smallholders, community gardens and schools in South Africa.

The three ethics

  • Earth care – look after soil, water, plants and animals.
  • People care – meet the needs of people: food, shelter, community.
  • Fair share – take only what you need and return surplus to the system and to others.

Key design principles and what they mean in practice

PrincipleFarm example
Observe and interactWatch where water flows, where frost settles and where the sun falls through a full year before planting
Catch and store energyHarvest rainwater from roofs into tanks; build swales to soak rain into the soil
Obtain a yieldMake sure the design produces food or income early, such as vegetables while fruit trees grow
Produce no wasteCompost kitchen scraps and manure; feed vegetable waste to chickens
Integrate rather than segregateChickens scratch and fertilise under fruit trees and eat pests
Use small and slow solutionsStart with one well-managed garden bed before expanding
Use and value diversityGrow many crops and varieties so one pest or drought does not destroy everything
Use edgesThe edge between a dam and land, or a hedge and a field, is rich in life and useful for planting
Creatively respond to changeAdjust plantings when rainfall patterns change

Every element in a permaculture design should serve more than one function, and every important function should be supported by more than one element. For example, a tree can give fruit, shade, mulch and a windbreak; water can come from both a borehole and a rainwater tank.

lessons.title: Illustrating a design: zones, sectors and water
lessons.html:
Zones: placing things by how often you visit them

A permaculture design places each element according to how often it needs attention. Imagine circles around the house:

  • Zone 0 – the house itself: water and energy saving, kitchen.
  • Zone 1 – right next to the house: herbs, salad greens, seedlings, compost, items used daily.
  • Zone 2 – a little further: small fruit trees, chickens, larger vegetable beds, beehives.
  • Zone 3 – main crops: maize, beans, pumpkins, orchards, larger livestock camps.
  • Zone 4 – semi-wild: grazing, woodlot for firewood and poles, wild foods.
  • Zone 5 – wild area left for nature, to observe and learn from.

On a sketch, draw these zones as rough rings or areas, and mark each element in its zone.

Sectors: energies from outside

Sectors are energies that come from outside the site: sun, wind, fire risk, flood water, noise, views and wild animals. On the sketch, draw arrows or wedges showing, for example, where the hot afternoon sun comes from, the direction of strong winds and where veld fires usually come from. Then place windbreaks, shade trees, firebreaks and buildings to use or block these energies.

Working with water

  • Swales – ditches dug along the contour with a mound on the downhill side. They slow and spread runoff so it soaks in, and trees are planted on the mound.
  • Rainwater tanks collecting from roofs.
  • Greywater from washing used carefully on fruit trees, not on leafy vegetables eaten raw.
  • Mulch to keep moisture in the soil.

Plant guilds

A guild is a group of plants that help each other around a central tree. For example, a fruit tree with comfrey (mulch and nutrients), nasturtiums (ground cover, attract insects), garlic or chives (pest deterrent) and beans (nitrogen). A well-known traditional guild is the three sisters: maize, beans and pumpkins grown together.

Key points

  • Permaculture follows three ethics: earth care, people care, fair share.
  • Design principles include observe, catch energy, no waste, integrate and value diversity.
  • Each element should have several functions, and each function several elements.
  • Zones place elements by how often they need attention; sectors map outside energies.
  • Swales, tanks, mulch and plant guilds make the design productive and resilient.
